name: Leg extension
angleNote: Knee flexion: 90° = lower leg hanging (start), 0° = leg straight (end). Lifting makes the angle smaller. Hip at the origin.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The lower leg includes the foot (combined centre of mass along knee → ankle; the foot's own position is approximated).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Hip→knee and knee→ankle in metres, typical adult.

strengthCurve.label: Knee extensor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric knee-extension torque vs knee flexion: weakest near full extension, peak about 65° (Anderson, tested 0–103°). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Lindahl et al. found the same shape (peak near 50°, about 50% of peak at 10°). Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m). Hip angle (two-joint rectus femoris) checked: no correction. Black et al. measured 139 Nm supine vs 140 Nm sitting, Bampouras et al. 245 vs 241 Nm; Worrell et al. found seated slightly stronger.
strengthCurve.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022; Lindahl O, Movin A, Ringqvist I (1969/1972). Isometric knee extension strength as a function of joint angle, muscle length and motor unit activity. Acta Orthop Scand 43:138–147; hip angle: Black SJ, Woodhouse ML, Suttmiller S, Shall L (1993). Influence of hip position on electromyographic and torque productions in the knee. J Sport Rehabil 2(1):26–34. doi:10.1123/jsr.2.1.26 (Table 1: 24 recreational athletes, isokinetic 30°/s); Bampouras TM, Reeves ND, Baltzopoulos V, Maganaris CN (2017). The role of agonist and antagonist muscles in explaining isometric knee extension torque variation with hip joint angle. Eur J Appl Physiol 117:2039–2045. doi:10.1007/s00421-017-3693-y; Worrell TW, Perrin DH, Denegar CR (1989). The influence of hip position on quadriceps and hamstring peak torque and reciprocal muscle group ratio values. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 11(3):104–107

muscles.name: Vasti (quadriceps)
muscles.note: Vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius: cross the knee only.

muscles.name: Rectus femoris (quadriceps)
muscles.note: Also crosses the hip; seated with the hip bent it is slack and contributes less. The weights here can't depend on hip angle.

phases.name: Lockout
phases.text: Leg nearly straight. An ankle weight is hardest here, exactly where the quads are weakest.

phases.name: Start
phases.text: Lower leg hanging. An ankle weight hangs almost under the knee, so there's little torque; a machine's cam can still load it.

variants.name: Leg extension machine (typical cam)

camProfile.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight. Shape: the mean of eight knee-extension machines from six makers, as % of its peak torque at knee angles 20–100° (Fig. 2B, read off; agrees with Table I within about 2 points), held flat below 20°. Scale: 0.30 m at the peak, nominal; the machines' absolute torque for a similar stack load differed widely (their Fig. 2A), so stack kg don't compare between machines or with free weights.
camProfile.source: Folland J, Morris B (2008). Variable-cam resistance training machines: do they match the angle–torque relationship in humans? J Sports Sci 26(2):163–169. doi:10.1080/02640410701370663

variants.notes: Pad on the shin near the ankle. The mean of eight measured machines stays within about 80–95% of its peak resistance across the range, while the quadriceps drop to about 40% of their peak near lockout (Folland & Morris: 75% at 100°, 40% at 20° of knee bend). So no machine matched the muscles: the effort still rises sharply towards lockout. The lower leg's own weight adds torque too.

variants.name: Machine: cam falling with knee bend (Strive S106, 2008)

camProfile.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight. Shape: the Strive S106 leg extension as measured in 2008, as % of its peak torque at knee angles 20–100° (Fig. 2B, read off; agrees with Table I within about 2 points), held flat below 20°. Scale: 0.30 m at the peak, nominal; the machines' absolute torque for a similar stack load differed widely (their Fig. 2A), so stack kg don't compare between machines or with free weights.
camProfile.source: Folland J, Morris B (2008). Variable-cam resistance training machines: do they match the angle–torque relationship in humans? J Sports Sci 26(2):163–169. doi:10.1080/02640410701370663

variants.notes: Resistance highest at lockout and falling as the knee bends (54% of peak at 100°): the opposite of the quadriceps' strength curve, so it is hardest exactly where the muscles are weakest. The machine as measured by Folland & Morris in 2008; current models may differ.

variants.name: Machine: cam rising with knee bend (Technogym Rehabilitation, 2008)

camProfile.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight. Shape: the Technogym Rehabilitation leg extension as measured in 2008, as % of its peak torque at knee angles 20–100° (Fig. 2B, read off; agrees with Table I within about 2 points), held flat below 20°. Scale: 0.30 m at the peak, nominal; the machines' absolute torque for a similar stack load differed widely (their Fig. 2A), so stack kg don't compare between machines or with free weights.
camProfile.source: Folland J, Morris B (2008). Variable-cam resistance training machines: do they match the angle–torque relationship in humans? J Sports Sci 26(2):163–169. doi:10.1080/02640410701370663

variants.notes: Resistance lowest near lockout (79% of peak at 20°) and highest with the knee bent: the closest to the muscles' ascending side, but still much flatter than their drop to 40% at lockout. The machine as measured by Folland & Morris in 2008; current models may differ.

variants.name: Seated knee extension with ankle weight
variants.notes: Gravity: torque = (m·L + lower-leg weight)·g·cos(knee angle). Zero with the lower leg hanging, largest at lockout.
